findings.outcome: The shared provider CLI reports schema-valid success after enforcing only a shallow subset of the supplied JSON Schema; shipped schemas rely on constraints the validator skips.
findings.severityImpact: high correctness and contract-integrity impact: an enum-violating, extra-property, malformed nested object, or wrong array item can be delivered as a successful verdict to consumers that trust the generic CLI envelope.
findings.confidence: high: source-confirmed on both final-message and submit-sidecar success paths, with shipped schemas using omitted keywords.
findings.fixRisk: medium: validation must remain dependency-free or introduce a deliberately supported validator without changing accepted output contracts unexpectedly.

evidence.excerpt: The validator checks object type, top-level required fields, and direct property type only, then returns ok.
validateSchemaSubset gates the final-message path immediately before successEnvelope.
The submit-sidecar path uses the same validator before returning the submitted verdict.
A shipped schema requires additionalProperties false, const, enum, nested required/properties, and array item constraints.

findings.whyCurrentBehaviorIsProblematic: The public prompt says the result must match the active JSON Schema, but the terminal validator does not enforce multiple constraints present in the product's own schemas. A response such as a string-valued enum field with an unsupported value and extra properties passes this gate if its top-level types happen to match.
findings.boundedFixSketch: Define the supported JSON-Schema profile and validate every keyword used by shipped schemas recursively (including const, enum, additionalProperties, nested required/properties, and items), or adopt a dependency-free generated validator for that profile. Add negative cases to both final-message and submit-sidecar paths.
findings.overlap: none found in current external plans or backlog items

findings.outcome: The shipped panel wrapper captures child stdout and stderr without a byte cap, unlike the hardened core wrapper it is documented as a twin of.
findings.severityImpact: high reliability impact: a noisy or compromised provider-CLI child can grow in-memory strings without bound, potentially exhausting the host process before the panel can record a controlled failure.
findings.confidence: high: source-confirmed divergence between panel and core implementations, plus the panel suite lacks the core's output-cap regression case.
findings.fixRisk: low to medium: port the existing bounded Buffer capture and forced-settlement behavior, preserving panel result/error types.

evidence.excerpt: stdout and stderr are concatenated on every data event; no byte accounting or cap-kill branch exists.
Each panelist invokes the provider CLI through this unbounded wrapper.
The core twin counts stream bytes, kills on cap breach, and schedules bounded settlement.
Core has a cap-plus-descendant regression test; the panel timeout suite has no equivalent cap test.

findings.whyCurrentBehaviorIsProblematic: The panel's sequential provider calls pass through a separate implementation that did not receive the core wrapper's output-cap hardening. Timeout support alone does not bound a fast, continuously writing child before its timeout, and normal panel invocation supplies no outer timeout value.
findings.boundedFixSketch: Extract or faithfully reuse the core bounded subprocess runner in the panel path; retain the 10 MiB per-stream policy, SIGKILL/final-resolution behavior, and structured cap error. Add the core's large-output and held-pipe cases to the panel suite.
findings.overlap: overlaps 2026-07-17-consensus-subprocess-hardening.md, whose declared scope included both wrapper copies; 2026-07-22-execution-program.md marks that plan done, so this is a residual/incomplete application rather than new duplicate scope. No specific open backlog item was found.

findings.outcome: The accepted request field redaction.include_stderr/include_args is validated but never applied when building provider result envelopes.
findings.severityImpact: medium security and API-contract impact: callers that explicitly request omitted stderr still receive provider stderr; provider diagnostics can contain sensitive or untrusted text.
findings.confidence: high that explicit redaction flags are currently inert; the intended default behavior when flags are omitted is not documented in the inspected sources.
findings.fixRisk: medium: suppressing fields by default could be a compatibility change, so preserve the current default unless the API contract explicitly changes and always honor explicit false.

evidence.excerpt: Request JSON parses and retains the validated redaction object.
Success and failure envelopes unconditionally copy supplied args, stdout, and stderr; they receive no redaction policy.

findings.whyCurrentBehaviorIsProblematic: An accepted API control creates an expectation that a caller can prevent stderr disclosure, yet the flag has no data-flow beyond validation. This is especially risky on failure paths, where raw provider stderr is included in the JSON envelope.
findings.boundedFixSketch: Thread the request redaction policy through success/failure envelope construction. Document a compatibility-preserving default and add tests proving explicit include_stderr:false removes stderr on both success and failure; similarly decide and test the args policy.
findings.overlap: none found in current external plans or backlog items

uncertainty: RUNTIME-003: the code proves explicit redaction flags are inert, but the desired default disclosure behavior is not specified in the inspected public runtime sources.

RUNTIME-001: some higher-level consumers add domain validation after the generic CLI returns, but the generic final-message and submit success gates themselves do not enforce the supplied full schema.
contradictions: The external subprocess-hardening plan says both core and panel wrapper copies were in scope and the execution program marks it done, but the current panel source lacks the core output-cap branch and its regression test.
gaps: Investigated without findings: provider host-recursion guard and child-environment filtering; core loop provider subprocess runner; consensus configuration parsing; session-observer collaboration lease path/permission checks; transcript export sanitizer and Cursor streaming parser.
